name: FLOW DIVERGENCE
subtitle: Stress–Fundamental Divergence
principle: Prices and fundamentals are coupled with a lag. When fear pushes price down while fundamentals are still improving, forward returns should be high; when price AND fundamentals break together, risk dominates.
intuition: Most frameworks look at price OR fundamentals. FLOW DIVERGENCE trades the disagreement between them — the moment investor psychology decouples from business reality.
math: DD_t = P_t / max(P_≤t) − 1   (stress: how far below the peak)
ΔE_t = E_t / E_{t−12} − 1   (fundamental direction: trailing earnings growth)
w_t = Trend_t; override w_t = 1 if DD_t ≤ θ and ΔE_t > 0 (stress + healthy fundamentals); force w_t = 0 if Trend_t = 0 and ΔE_t < 0 (both broken)
Decided at month-end t, applied in t+1 (no look-ahead). θ = −10%.
inputs: (v2) Earnings yield − 10Y yield vs its 20-year median
rules: Divergence buy: price ≥10% off highs while earnings still growing → stay invested.
Confirmation sell: below trend AND earnings falling → cash.
portfolio: Index-level: 100% equities or 100% T-bills. Stock-level version (untested): rank stocks by drawdown × positive estimate revisions.
exits: Earnings growth turns negative while below trend
Drawdown recovers above trend (override no longer needed)
failure: Earnings data lags (reported quarterly, revised) — the 'healthy fundamentals' you see may already be stale.
Crises where earnings fall after prices (2008): the override keeps you in too long.
verdict: REJECTED (as a new edge). v1 behaved 86% like plain trend following (return correlation 0.87) and did not beat it out-of-sample (Sharpe 0.83 vs 0.84). The 'stress + healthy earnings' state was the WORST stress state in 1900–1979 and the best in 1980–2023 — an unstable relationship, not a law. v2 (equity-risk-premium gate) was worse than trend (0.75 vs 0.89). FLOW did not force a success.
break_it: Barely. 86% of months had the same position as the 10-month trend rule.
Is it secretly an existing factor?
Yes — mostly time-series momentum/trend, with a valuation-ish tilt in v2.
θ sensitivity was flat (test Sharpe 0.77–0.90 across −5% to −30%), so not fragile — just not better.
The 1980–2023 'stress + healthy earnings' 98% hit rate is hindsight-prone: few independent episodes (≈5 bear markets).
Conditional forward returns flipped between periods. Fails.
Helps in slow bear markets, hurts in fast earnings-led crashes.
Not better than the simpler rule.

theory.idea: Edges live where human behavior forces prices away from reality — but the simplest description of that behavior (trend) already captures most of it at the index level.
theory.method: Hypothesis → rules → 126 years of data → train/test split → walk-forward → parameter sensitivity → red team → accept/reject. Failed ideas are kept.
theory.evidence: Trend following was the only index rule that survived every test: OOS Sharpe 0.89 vs 0.63, max drawdown −19% vs −49%, every parameter from 3–24 months beat buy-and-hold OOS, walk-forward Sharpe 0.77 vs 0.50 since 1920. Its gain is risk control, not higher returns.
theory.weaknesses: Monthly index data only; no point-in-time stock fundamentals; few independent bear markets; dividends frozen after 2023; WTI used as swing proxy.
theory.next: Test FLOW DIVERGENCE at the STOCK level with point-in-time analyst estimate revisions (price drawdown × upward revisions), where the disagreement between price and fundamentals is far more frequent than at index level.
